lesson_title: The City That Watched Its Dams Run Out
hook_text: For seven years the rain kept missing one South African city. By 2022 its dams were at one-tenth.
clip_script: When drought corners a modern city, it looks like Nelson Mandela Bay. Season after season from about 2015, the rains missed the Eastern Cape catchments that fill the metro's dams. By the winter of 2022 the combined supply had slumped toward one-tenth, the big Kouga Dam was nearly out of the game, and Gqeberha was drawing up maps of water collection points for the day the taps failed. Here is what makes this geography and not just a headline: drought is never simply low rainfall — Springbok lives happily on two hundred millimetres a year. Drought is a place's own normal failing, and it collapses in a fixed order: first the rain, then the soil, then the rivers and dams, then jobs, prices and daily life. The metro was standing at the last stage. So it fought on every front at once — mains pressure turned down, leak crews chasing the water that never reached a tap, emergency boreholes, extra Orange River water hurried in through the Nooitgedagt scheme, and every resident pushed toward fifty litres a day. One filled bath is more than that. The taps, just barely, stayed open until the 2023 rains lifted the siege. Hold both halves of the story: the danger was completely real, and determined management genuinely held it off.
visual_style: Dam-level gauges sliding toward a red one-tenth mark over drone shots of cracked mud, a city map sprouting collection-point pins, then repair crews, boreholes and a pipeline arrow from the Orange River as the gauge steadies and green returns.
mood: True-story tension resolved by stubborn collective effort.
pacing: Slow ominous open on the failing seasons, methodical middle through the four stages, quickening beat of countermeasures to a steadied close.
